paragraphs.heading: From egg to embryo
paragraphs.text: Animal embryonic development, also called embryogenesis, is the stage when an animal is an embryo. It starts when a sperm cell fertilizes an egg cell, or ovum. The fertilized egg becomes a single cell called a zygote. In mammals the term mostly covers the early stages before birth, while the words fetus and fetal development name the later ones.

paragraphs.heading: Fertilization
paragraphs.text: Fertilization is the joining of gametes to make a new organism; in animals, a sperm fuses with an ovum. Depending on the species, this happens inside the female's body, called internal fertilization, or outside it, called external fertilization. The egg also has to stop more than one sperm getting in, which is called polyspermy. First comes a fast block: right after one sperm fertilizes the egg, the electrical charge across its membrane rapidly shifts and then returns to normal. A slow block begins within the first few seconds, as released calcium makes granules in the egg release enzymes that cause its outer membrane to swell and harden, keeping other sperm out.

paragraphs.heading: Cleavage
paragraphs.text: Next comes cleavage: the zygote divides again and again by mitosis without growing, so the cluster of cells stays the size of the original zygote. At least four divisions take place, giving a tightly packed ball of sixteen or more cells, called the morula. The cells made by cleavage, up to the blastula stage, are called blastomeres. Once the seventh division has produced 128 cells, the morula has become a blastula.

paragraphs.heading: Not every animal divides alike
paragraphs.text: Cleavage does not look the same in every animal. In holoblastic cleavage, all the cells divide, the division furrow runs across the whole cluster, and the whole cluster ends up as the embryo. In meroblastic cleavage only some cells divide, as the furrow does not reach into the yolky region, and some cells become the yolk sac. Animals also differ in the geometry of the furrow, which can be radial, spiral, bilateral or rotational.

paragraphs.heading: Blastula, gastrula and beyond
paragraphs.text: A blastula is usually a ball made of a single sheet of cells, the blastoderm, around a cavity filled with fluid or yolk called the blastocoel. Mammals at this point form a blastocyst, which has an inner cell mass set apart from the surrounding ball. In most animal groups the blastula then goes through gastrulation and becomes a gastrula, which has two cell layers in some species and three in most. The gastrula develops further, including organogenesis, the forming of organs. The embryo then moves on to its next stage, which differs between species: a fetus or a larva, for example.
